title: Arcy Drive’s ‘Attic Rock’ Is Taking the Music World by Storm
summary:
"The attic's never finished," says Nick Mateyunas, frontman of Arcy Drive. "You can see exposed wood, and there's stuff in it that you can't get rid of, but it still holds value. It sticks around, and you don't even know why. That's what we are." This philosophy defines "attic rock," the label Arcy Drive chose for their sound — a blend of angsty emo and classic garage rock.

The four-piece band from Long Island consists of Mateyunas (vocals, guitar), Brooke Tuozzo (drums), Austin Jones (guitar), and Patrick Helrigel (bass). They met in school in Northport, New York, and started playing covers just before the pandemic. Only Tuozzo had a musical background, so the others spent the first year catching up. But Mateyunas, inspired by Neil Young and Nirvana, was determined to write original songs.

Their big break came through social media. In 2021-2022, they posted videos of themselves converting a decommissioned school bus into a tour bus, which endeared them to fans. Songs like "Roll My Stone" and "Superbloomer" went viral, leading to festival slots at Lollapalooza and Bonnaroo in 2023. Their track "Louie," written for Mateyunas's grandfather (who calls everyone "Louie" because he forgets names), became a fan favorite and a defining moment at the 2026 Bonnaroo.

Their 2025 album The Pit amplified their live shows, transforming them from "rowdy to real rowdy," according to Jones. The band recently wrapped up a tour of sold-out venues like New York's Webster Hall and the Troubadour in West Hollywood. Upcoming plans include a July 4 performance at Rolling Stone's Stateside Festival, opening slots for Mt. Joy at Red Rocks, and a European tour in September. Mateyunas says their next album will be "an extension of myself," adding, "I can't wait to get rid of it to move on."
why_it_matters: Arcy Drive’s rise shows how authenticity and a little creativity — even converting an old bus into home on the road — can launch a career without traditional industry gatekeepers. For teens, it demonstrates that the path from a school band to festival stages is possible through community building and taking risks online.

background_read: Arcy Drive is part of a modern wave of indie bands that built their audience through social media rather than traditional record labels. Platforms like TikTok and Instagram allow musicians to share both music and behind-the-scenes content, which can turn a local act into a festival headliner.

The band’s breakthrough festival appearances at Lollapalooza (Chicago’s massive multi-genre event, running since 1991) and Bonnaroo (a Tennessee camping festival famous for eclectic lineups) placed them alongside established stars and exposed them to tens of thousands of new listeners.

Their 'attic rock' label is a creative way to define a sound that blends emo (a heart-on-sleeve rock subgenre) with garage rock (raw, unpolished energy), much like earlier 2000s acts who fused catchy tunes with a DIY ethic.

Long Island, where they grew up, has a long musical history — from the punk of The Ramones to the indie storytelling of Bayside — though the band’s Northport roots are more suburban, far from the typical big-city music scene.

Selling out venues like Webster Hall (a historic New York concert hall dating from 1886) and the Troubadour (a legendary West Hollywood club that helped launch Elton John and James Taylor) signals that Arcy Drive is moving quickly into the mainstream.

perspectives.description: The band’s success story is a testament to grassroots fandom: fans felt personally invested after watching the bus conversion and hearing vulnerable lyrics like 'Louie.' Their rapid climb is a win for indie music and proves social media can reward substance over polish.

Building a career on viral moments creates pressure to constantly produce content, which can burn out young artists. The jump from small clubs to huge festivals so quickly may also leave them without the time to develop stagecraft organically, and a few under-attended gigs could derail momentum.

Arcy Drive follows a pattern seen in the early 2000s garage revival but adds modern digital marketing. Their 'attic rock' is less a new genre than a clever rebranding of emo and garage influences, showing how labels shape perception even when the sound is familiar.

The next album will be crucial in determining if they can move beyond a curated online presence into a lasting career. Their European tour will test whether their appeal translates outside the U.S., and the Red Rocks opening slot is a high-stakes chance to convert mainstream rock fans.
